forceToolCall.description:
Run the step as one model call with the tool choice pinned to this capability, instead of calling it
        straight from the runtime. The model still cannot decide *whether* to call it — only what to put in the
        arguments left unpinned, which is what a lookup keyed on something nobody can template ('the symptom the
        caller just described') needs.

        Costs one model call where the default costs none, so it is opt-in. Honoured where the action has
        arguments a model can write — `tool`, `connector`, `agent`, and a `transfer` whose target the model
        chooses; ignored elsewhere. Leaving it false while a required argument is unpinned is an authoring error,
        not a runtime one: nothing would be there to fill it.

output.description:
Workflow variable the action's result is written to, so later `expression` conditions can branch on it and
        later steps can template it (e.g. capture a lookup into `policy`, then branch on
        `{ "==": [{ "var": "policy.status" }, "active"] }`). Absent means the result is not captured; the
        model still sees it in the conversation per the capability's own pipeline.

        Written on success only. A failed action leaves the variable as it was and takes a `failure` transition
        instead — see AgentWorkflowFailureCondition — so a graph can never mistake an error for a result.

variables.description: Write workflow variables. The step nobody asks for until the first time a graph has to remember something between two branches.

items.description: One `name = value` write. Exactly one of `value` or `expression` is set: `value` renders text, `expression` computes.

value.description: Text written to the variable, with handlebars resolved against workflow variables, agent variables and session context (e.g. '{{lookup.status}}'). Empty clears the variable.

expression.description: A JsonLogic expression computing the value instead of rendering it, which is what makes arithmetic possible: `{ "+": [{ "var": "attempts" }, 1] }` is the retry counter a bounded loop needs, written with no model in the loop.

workflow.description:
Run a nested workflow and continue once it returns.

    The unit of decomposition: a twelve-step identity check is called from the front door, from the booking flow
    and from the complaints line, so it is authored once and referenced by a single step at each call site. The
    nested workflow shares this session and its variables; it returns through its `result` steps, which is what
    the calling step's `result` transitions branch on. A nested workflow that instead reaches an `end` or a
    terminal action does what it says — the session is over and nothing comes back.
The nested workflow to run. Must be declared in `AgentWorkflow.nested`, and must not run itself directly or through a ring of nested workflows.

output.description: Workflow variable the nested workflow's result `value` is written to. Absent means the value is discarded — which is the usual case when the branch taken is the whole answer.

result.description:
End this workflow and hand control back to whatever invoked it.

    In a nested workflow the invoking step resumes and branches on which result was reached (see
    AgentWorkflowResultCondition). In the main graph of a workflow-channel agent the run finishes and the result
    is returned to the caller — the agent, automation or API request that started it. In the main graph of a
    voice / chat / assistant agent there is no invoker, so it behaves as `end`.

value.description: What this result returns to the invoker. Supports handlebars resolved against workflow variables, agent variables and session context (e.g. '{{policy.number}}'). Absent returns the result's id alone, which is enough when the caller only branches on which result was reached.

end.description: The session is over. Terminal and configuration-free by design: a closing line is a `message` step in front of it, and releasing a call is the `hangup` action — both already exist, and neither needs restating here.

items.description: One way out of a step.

target.description: Step to move to. Must be a step of the same workflow — a nested workflow is entered through a `workflow` step, not by pointing a transition into it.

condition.description: How the runtime decides to take a transition. Exactly one member is set.

always.description: Unconditional. Only legal as a step's single transition: two unconditional exits are a coin toss, not a routing decision.

prompt.description:
A condition the model judges against the conversation, e.g. 'the caller has said they will try the fix'.

    Phrase it as something the **caller** has done. A condition describing what the *agent* has done — 'the
    caller has a next step to try' — is true the instant the agent names one, so the model leaves before the
    caller has answered, and one early exit cascades through the rest of the graph. Rewording the same exits from
    agent actions to caller actions, changing nothing else, moved three models from 58–64 % of turns on the right
    step to 96–100 %, and removed every stray move. It is the single largest effect measured on this contract, so
    an authoring surface that accepts an agent-action condition is the defect, not the wording.

expression.description: A branch taken when workflow state satisfies the condition — no model judgement involved, which is what makes it the right condition after an `action` or `variables` step.

conditions.description:
A JsonLogic condition tree evaluated against workflow state, e.g.
    `{ "==": [ { "var": "lookup.status" }, "found" ] }`. The `var` namespace is the workflow variables
    written by `variables` steps and action `output` captures, the agent's input variables
    (`engine.ai.variables`), and the session context. An empty tree always matches. This is a
    separate language from the rule-tree AutomationConditions (wilma-workflows) and CopilotConditions
    (wilma-copilot).

result.description: A branch on which result a nested workflow returned. Only meaningful on a `workflow` step; the referenced step must be a `result` step of the nested workflow that step runs.
Id of the `result` step reached inside the nested workflow. An id rather than a name, so renaming a result from 'failed' to 'gave up' does not unwire every step that handles it.

failure.description:
A branch taken when the step's action fails. Only meaningful on an `action` step, and the only condition a
    terminal action may carry: a transfer that finds the extension busy has not left the session, so a graph that
    cannot say what happens next simply drops the caller.

    Failure short-circuits — when an action fails, only `failure` transitions are considered, never the
    `expression` or `prompt` branches that were written for its result. If none matches, the session fails with
    the action's error, so a step whose capability can fail wants a catch-all last in the list.

items.description:
How an action failed, as far as the runtime can tell. Deliberately a short list of kinds an author can write
    a different recovery for — a busy extension is a different flow from an expired credential — rather than a
    mirror of every provider's error codes. The message and the provider's own detail stay on the invocation
    event and the trace; a graph branches on the kind.

kinds.description: Kinds this branch handles, evaluated as a set. Absent or empty catches **any** failure — the catch-all, which the list order must therefore place after the specific branches.

fallback.description: The else-branch, taken when no sibling matched. At most one per step, and reached last regardless of where it sits in the list.

transitions.description:
The ways out of this step. Must be non-empty on every step that stays in the session, since a step the
        runtime cannot leave is a dead end.

        On `result` and `end` it must be empty. On the `action` members that leave the session (`handover`,
        `delegation`, `transfer`, `hangup`) it may carry `failure` transitions and nothing else: an action that
        was supposed to leave and failed — a busy extension, a service desk with nobody on it — has not left, and
        a graph with no answer for that drops the caller.

position.description: Canvas coordinates of a step in the builder. Authoring metadata: the runtime ignores it, and a workflow that arrives without positions is laid out automatically.

steps.description: Steps of one graph. Ids are unique within it.

items.description: A named graph the main workflow — or another nested workflow — can run, referenced by AgentWorkflowInvokeHandler.

entry.description: Step the graph starts at. Must be one of `steps`.

id.description: Identifier of a step within its workflow, unique per workflow (the main graph and each nested workflow are separate scopes). Stable and machine-facing: transitions reference it, and a result step's id is the name a caller branches on, so renaming a step's `label` never unwires the graph.

label.description:
Human readable name of a step, e.g. 'Transfer to the sales desk'. Shown in the builder and in traces, and
    read by the model too: when this step is an exit of the live step, the label is the preview offered alongside
    the exit's condition. Never a routing key — see AgentWorkflowStepId — so renaming one never unwires a graph.

stage.description: The phase this step belongs to. Inherited by steps downstream, so a handful of tags organise a long graph.

handler.description: What a step does. Exactly one member is set. `action` carries a capability; the others are workflow-only handlers with no capability equivalent.

conversation.description:
A stretch of conversation with a goal: the model talks, may use the capabilities in scope, and the step's
    transitions are evaluated against what happens. This is the only handler that leaves control where it is
    until a transition matches — a step whose conditions all stay false simply keeps talking.

    Deliberately not configurable per step: the model, and how readily the step is left. The model is the
    agent's (`engine.ai.model`) because a session that swaps models mid-conversation swaps voice, latency and
    tool-calling behaviour with it. How readily a step is left is decided by how its transitions are worded —
    conditions describing what the *caller* has done keep a model on the step, and no eagerness dial moves that
    number.

goal.description: What the agent is trying to achieve here, appended to the agent's `engine.ai.instructions`. Never a replacement for them: identity, tone and standing rules hold across every step, and a step that needs different ones is a different agent.

channels.description: Per-channel settings of a conversation step. Only voice has anything to say about a stretch of conversation today; the chat and assistant surfaces deliver it as they deliver every other reply.

capabilities.description:
Capabilities offered to the model *in addition* to `engine.ai.capabilities` while this step runs,
        configured exactly as they are there — the same union, the same structures. Use it to give a step reach
        it should not have everywhere: authoring the refund tool on the refund step, rather than on the agent, is
        also what keeps it out of every other step.

        Additive only, by design. A step cannot drop an agent-level capability, so it cannot strand a session by
        taking away the `handover` or `transfer` its channel needs, and the runtime keeps one rule for the turn's
        tool set. Skills the model loads (`engine.ai.skills`) and the channel's own built-ins join it either way.

message.description: Say one thing — spoken on voice, posted on chat / assistant — then move on. The line is either authored verbatim or generated at the step; either way the agent says it once and the transitions are evaluated, with no turn handed to the user.

content.description: Where the step's line comes from. Exactly one member is set: `text` is authored, `generate` is written by the model at the step.

text.description: The line, verbatim. No model in the loop, which is what makes it the right content for a disclosure, a policy sentence or a legally worded confirmation.

channels.description: Per-channel settings of a message step: how the line is protected when spoken, and what is offered with it when posted.

action.description:
A step that performs one capability. The runtime performs it on arrival — no model decision about *whether*
    to act, and no tool offered to the model for it. Which is the point: an action the graph reached is an action
    that happens, at the cost of nothing.

capability.description:
The capability a step performs, run by the runtime rather than chosen by the model. A subset of
    AgentCapability, reusing its structures verbatim: these are the members that describe a single action with a
    beginning and an end. The rest of AgentCapability (`kb`, `webSearch`, `webFetch`, `sandbox`, `suggestions`)
    describes reach the model draws on while it talks, so it belongs on a conversation step's `capabilities`
    rather than on a step of its own.

    Configuration comes from the capability itself and nothing is added here: a tool step's fixed arguments are
    `AgentTool.fields` predefined handlers, its spoken lead-in is `AgentTool.startMessage`, a transfer's line
    before the hand-off is `AgentTransferPipeline.instructions`, an invoked agent's inputs are
    `AgentCallCapability.variables`. Anything left unpinned is filled by the model at the step, per the tool's
    input schema.

forceToolCall.description:
Run the step as one model call with the tool choice pinned to this capability, instead of calling it
        straight from the runtime. The model still cannot decide *whether* to call it — only what to put in the
        arguments left unpinned, which is what a lookup keyed on something nobody can template ('the symptom the
        caller just described') needs.

        Costs one model call where the default costs none, so it is opt-in. Honoured where the action has
        arguments a model can write — `tool`, `connector`, `agent`, and a `transfer` whose target the model
        chooses; ignored elsewhere. Leaving it false while a required argument is unpinned is an authoring error,
        not a runtime one: nothing would be there to fill it.

output.description:
Workflow variable the action's result is written to, so later `expression` conditions can branch on it and
        later steps can template it (e.g. capture a lookup into `policy`, then branch on
        `{ "==": [{ "var": "policy.status" }, "active"] }`). Absent means the result is not captured; the
        model still sees it in the conversation per the capability's own pipeline.

        Written on success only. A failed action leaves the variable as it was and takes a `failure` transition
        instead — see AgentWorkflowFailureCondition — so a graph can never mistake an error for a result.

variables.description: Write workflow variables. The step nobody asks for until the first time a graph has to remember something between two branches.

items.description: One `name = value` write. Exactly one of `value` or `expression` is set: `value` renders text, `expression` computes.

value.description: Text written to the variable, with handlebars resolved against workflow variables, agent variables and session context (e.g. '{{lookup.status}}'). Empty clears the variable.

expression.description: A JsonLogic expression computing the value instead of rendering it, which is what makes arithmetic possible: `{ "+": [{ "var": "attempts" }, 1] }` is the retry counter a bounded loop needs, written with no model in the loop.

workflow.description:
Run a nested workflow and continue once it returns.

    The unit of decomposition: a twelve-step identity check is called from the front door, from the booking flow
    and from the complaints line, so it is authored once and referenced by a single step at each call site. The
    nested workflow shares this session and its variables; it returns through its `result` steps, which is what
    the calling step's `result` transitions branch on. A nested workflow that instead reaches an `end` or a
    terminal action does what it says — the session is over and nothing comes back.
The nested workflow to run. Must be declared in `AgentWorkflow.nested`, and must not run itself directly or through a ring of nested workflows.

output.description: Workflow variable the nested workflow's result `value` is written to. Absent means the value is discarded — which is the usual case when the branch taken is the whole answer.

result.description:
End this workflow and hand control back to whatever invoked it.

    In a nested workflow the invoking step resumes and branches on which result was reached (see
    AgentWorkflowResultCondition). In the main graph of a workflow-channel agent the run finishes and the result
    is returned to the caller — the agent, automation or API request that started it. In the main graph of a
    voice / chat / assistant agent there is no invoker, so it behaves as `end`.

value.description: What this result returns to the invoker. Supports handlebars resolved against workflow variables, agent variables and session context (e.g. '{{policy.number}}'). Absent returns the result's id alone, which is enough when the caller only branches on which result was reached.

end.description: The session is over. Terminal and configuration-free by design: a closing line is a `message` step in front of it, and releasing a call is the `hangup` action — both already exist, and neither needs restating here.

items.description: One way out of a step.

target.description: Step to move to. Must be a step of the same workflow — a nested workflow is entered through a `workflow` step, not by pointing a transition into it.

condition.description: How the runtime decides to take a transition. Exactly one member is set.

always.description: Unconditional. Only legal as a step's single transition: two unconditional exits are a coin toss, not a routing decision.

prompt.description:
A condition the model judges against the conversation, e.g. 'the caller has said they will try the fix'.

    Phrase it as something the **caller** has done. A condition describing what the *agent* has done — 'the
    caller has a next step to try' — is true the instant the agent names one, so the model leaves before the
    caller has answered, and one early exit cascades through the rest of the graph. Rewording the same exits from
    agent actions to caller actions, changing nothing else, moved three models from 58–64 % of turns on the right
    step to 96–100 %, and removed every stray move. It is the single largest effect measured on this contract, so
    an authoring surface that accepts an agent-action condition is the defect, not the wording.

expression.description: A branch taken when workflow state satisfies the condition — no model judgement involved, which is what makes it the right condition after an `action` or `variables` step.

conditions.description:
A JsonLogic condition tree evaluated against workflow state, e.g.
    `{ "==": [ { "var": "lookup.status" }, "found" ] }`. The `var` namespace is the workflow variables
    written by `variables` steps and action `output` captures, the agent's input variables
    (`engine.ai.variables`), and the session context. An empty tree always matches. This is a
    separate language from the rule-tree AutomationConditions (wilma-workflows) and CopilotConditions
    (wilma-copilot).

result.description: A branch on which result a nested workflow returned. Only meaningful on a `workflow` step; the referenced step must be a `result` step of the nested workflow that step runs.
Id of the `result` step reached inside the nested workflow. An id rather than a name, so renaming a result from 'failed' to 'gave up' does not unwire every step that handles it.

failure.description:
A branch taken when the step's action fails. Only meaningful on an `action` step, and the only condition a
    terminal action may carry: a transfer that finds the extension busy has not left the session, so a graph that
    cannot say what happens next simply drops the caller.

    Failure short-circuits — when an action fails, only `failure` transitions are considered, never the
    `expression` or `prompt` branches that were written for its result. If none matches, the session fails with
    the action's error, so a step whose capability can fail wants a catch-all last in the list.

kinds.description: Kinds this branch handles, evaluated as a set. Absent or empty catches **any** failure — the catch-all, which the list order must therefore place after the specific branches.

fallback.description: The else-branch, taken when no sibling matched. At most one per step, and reached last regardless of where it sits in the list.

transitions.description:
The ways out of this step. Must be non-empty on every step that stays in the session, since a step the
        runtime cannot leave is a dead end.

        On `result` and `end` it must be empty. On the `action` members that leave the session (`handover`,
        `delegation`, `transfer`, `hangup`) it may carry `failure` transitions and nothing else: an action that
        was supposed to leave and failed — a busy extension, a service desk with nobody on it — has not left, and
        a graph with no answer for that drops the caller.

position.description: Canvas coordinates of a step in the builder. Authoring metadata: the runtime ignores it, and a workflow that arrives without positions is laid out automatically.

steps.description: Steps of one graph. Ids are unique within it.

id.description: Identifier of a nested workflow within the agent's workflow.

description.description: One line saying what the nested workflow is for, shown on the step that runs it.

nested.description: Graphs the main workflow can run, referenced by `workflow` steps.

maxTransitions.description:
Give up after this many step transitions, so a cycle whose conditions all keep matching cannot run
        forever. Absent means no limit, which is the default: a deliberate loop — 'keep asking until you have the
        postcode' — is a normal shape, and silently capping it would be worse than making the author say so.

items.description: One `name = value` write. Exactly one of `value` or `expression` is set: `value` renders text, `expression` computes.

value.description: Text written to the variable, with handlebars resolved against workflow variables, agent variables and session context (e.g. '{{lookup.status}}'). Empty clears the variable.

expression.description: A JsonLogic expression computing the value instead of rendering it, which is what makes arithmetic possible: `{ "+": [{ "var": "attempts" }, 1] }` is the retry counter a bounded loop needs, written with no model in the loop.

variables.description: Workflow variables seeded before the first step runs. Agent input variables (`engine.ai.variables`) are already in scope and need no entry here.

layout.description: How the builder arranges the graph. Authoring metadata: the runtime ignores it. `stages` bands the graph by `stage`, which is what a forty-step workflow needs.

guardrails.description: Turn screening, by side. Only `input` exists: it guards what reaches the model, and output screening is a separate policy with different actions, added here when it is built.

input.description:
Screening applied to what reaches the model.

    There is deliberately no bundle or preset-group member. A named group that expands to a set of checks
    reads like convenience and behaves like version skew: the same agent definition would mean different
    things before and after a platform release, invisibly to the tenant who published it. Listing the checks
    costs a few lines in a document the console writes anyway, and the published version then states exactly
    what it enforces.

    There is also no set-level default action. One field standing behind every check reads as a convenience
    and hides the thing a reader most needs to see: what a given check will actually do. A check's action is
    its own or its preset's, and both are visible on the check.

items.description:
One thing the checker is asked about a turn. There is deliberately no `enabled` flag: a check that
    should not run is removed, so a published version never carries a switched-off check that reads like
    policy.

name.description: Name of a check, unique within a guardrail set. Stable and machine-facing: session events and trace spans report a verdict by this name, so a reader needs no copy of the agent definition to tell which check fired.

kind.description: What a check is: one of the platform's presets, or a prompt the tenant wrote. Exactly one member is set.

preset.description: A check backed by one of the platform's prebuilt prompts.

A prebuilt check. Each preset is a platform-maintained prompt shipped in code and versioned with the
    platform, not a tenant row — so a support question about what a preset caught has one answer. A preset
    check is otherwise an ordinary AgentGuardrailCheck: its sensitivity and action are the tenant's to set,
    and `notes` narrows its prompt without replacing it.

notes.description: Appended to the preset's prompt. For narrowing, not redefining — 'ignore card numbers read back after our own IVR prompts for them' — so the preset keeps its maintenance while fitting a tenant whose product would otherwise fight it.

custom.description: A check written by the tenant. A name and a prompt is the whole surface: no category enum can express the rules customers actually buy, such as refusing to quote a price before qualifying.

instructions.description: Natural-language description of what a custom check looks for. Describe the *content* to be caught, not an instruction to the checker: 'The caller is asking about cryptocurrency investments' works, 'Block all content about crypto' does not, and a negative definition ('anything except billing questions') reliably misfires.

sensitivity.description:
How much confidence a verdict needs before it counts as tripped. The checker reports a confidence per
    check and this is the threshold against it, so raising sensitivity catches more and costs more false
    positives without changing the prompt or the model: `low` trips only on high confidence, `medium` on
    high and medium, `high` on anything but a clear pass. Defaults to MEDIUM.

action.description:
What happens when a check trips. Exactly one member is set.

    Ordered by severity: observe < redact < block < end. When more than one check trips in the same call the
    most severe action wins and ties break on the order of `checks`, so a set can mix an observed check with
    an enforced one without the observation weakening the enforcement.

    There is no hand-over member yet. Handing a session to a human is a different mechanism on every channel
    — a voice transfer, a chat assignment, an assistant with no human behind it — and wiring a guardrail into
    all of them is out of proportion to the rest of this feature. Until AgentHandoverCapability has a runtime
    on more than one channel, the crisis path is a block whose message routes the caller.

observe.description: Record the verdict and let the turn through. The rollout mode: every guardrail should run here first, against real traffic, until its trips are read and its sensitivity is tuned. A tripped check still emits GuardrailTrippedEvent and still appears in the trace, which is what makes this a tuning tool rather than a switched-off check.

redact.description: Mask the matched spans and let the turn continue. The mask is chosen by the platform and is not configurable — a tenant-authored placeholder that collides with real text, or that the model reads as an instruction, is worse than having no choice. Only valid on checks that return spans (PII, SECRETS).

block.description: Refuse the turn. The agent's model is never called, no tool runs, and the caller is answered with `message` instead. The session stays alive and the conversation continues, so on a check meant to redirect rather than stop — 'let me take a few details first' — the message is doing the work.

message.description: Said to the caller in place of the agent's reply. Falls back to a channel default when unset.

end.description: End the session. It lands in SessionStatus TERMINATED — not STOPPED, which is what a user asking to stop means — so a refused session is never read back as a clean finish. On voice this hangs up the call; on the other channels the session simply accepts no further turns.

message.description: Said to the caller before the session ends.

checks.description: The checks to run, evaluated together in one call. Absent or empty means no screening.

model.description: The model that runs the checks. Defaults to the platform's guardrail model — deliberately small and fast, and deliberately not the agent's own, whose cost and latency are what this exists to avoid spending on a bad turn.

action.description:
What happens when a check trips. Exactly one member is set.

    Ordered by severity: observe < redact < block < end. When more than one check trips in the same call the
    most severe action wins and ties break on the order of `checks`, so a set can mix an observed check with
    an enforced one without the observation weakening the enforcement.

    There is no hand-over member yet. Handing a session to a human is a different mechanism on every channel
    — a voice transfer, a chat assignment, an assistant with no human behind it — and wiring a guardrail into
    all of them is out of proportion to the rest of this feature. Until AgentHandoverCapability has a runtime
    on more than one channel, the crisis path is a block whose message routes the caller.

A tripped check still emits GuardrailTrippedEvent and still appears in the trace, which is what makes this a tuning tool rather than a switched-off check.

The mask is chosen by the platform and is not configurable — a tenant-authored placeholder that collides with real text, or that the model reads as an instruction, is worse than having no choice. Only valid on checks that return spans (PII, SECRETS).

The session stays alive and the conversation continues, so on a check meant to redirect rather than stop — 'let me take a few details first' — the message is doing the work.

message.description: Said to the caller in place of the agent's reply. Falls back to a channel default when unset.

end.description: End the session. It lands in SessionStatus TERMINATED — not STOPPED, which is what a user asking to stop means — so a refused session is never read back as a clean finish. On voice this hangs up the call; on the other channels the session simply accepts no further turns.

message.description: Said to the caller before the session ends.

mode.description: Runs the checker before the agent's model (BLOCKING) or alongside it (PARALLEL). Blocking costs the checker's latency on every turn but guarantees that a refused turn spent no tokens and fired no tool; parallel adds no latency and is the right trade on voice, where the delay is audible, at the risk that part of a reply reaches the caller and that a tool has already run before the cancellation lands. Defaults to BLOCKING.

errorMode.description: What happens when the checker itself errors or times out. OPEN lets the turn through unscreened and records GuardrailFailedEvent, so an unscreened turn is a fact in the log rather than an absence; CLOSED refuses it. Defaults to OPEN: an agent that stops answering because a small model had a bad minute is a worse and far likelier outage than the rare turn that goes unscreened. Background tasks, where nobody is waiting and a retry is free, are the case for CLOSED.

window.description: How much of the conversation the checker sees. Defaults to LAST_WITH_PRIOR, because the jailbreaks worth catching are built across several turns — establish a fiction, then cash it in — and a checker shown only the last turn sees an innocuous sentence. There is no full-transcript option: screening a whole call on every turn would make the guardrail dearer than the agent.

model.description: Defaults to the platform default model when omitted.

timeZone.description: IANA timezone the agent reasons about time in: it anchors the current date and time given to the model and how times are read from and written to tool arguments and replies. Shared by every channel the agent serves. Defaults to 'UTC'.

artifacts.description: Whether the agent can produce artifacts (wilma-artifacts): files it writes in its sandbox and shares back during a session — a document, a PDF, a spreadsheet, a chart, a multi-page web site, a folder of files. Needs the sandbox capability. An artifact starts private to the user the session runs for, who can share it company-wide from the viewer; on the chat channel the runtime shares each one company-wide as it is created, so the link posted into the conversation opens for every signed-in colleague. Artifacts are company-internal: recipients on external transports (sms / whatsapp) or outside the company cannot open the links, so keep this disabled for customer-facing agents. Defaults to false.

items.description: Reference to a skill attached to an agent.

skillVersion.description: Pin a specific published skill version. When omitted, latestVersion is resolved.

access.description:
Who is allowed to use the agent. There is no view/edit dimension — access solely grants the ability to use the agent.

    Where it is applied, per channel:
    - `assistant` — enforced. GetAgent on wilma-assistant refuses an agent the caller is not granted.
    - `voice` — deliberately not applied. Inbound calls are routed by the PBX dialplan, and the data ACL is the
      agent-level `settings.pbxGroupId`, not per-user grants.
    - `chat` — enforced for COLLEAGUES ONLY. wilma-chat checks the sender against this block when the sender
      belongs to the agent's own company. A sender from outside it — a Kite website visitor, an SMS or WhatsApp
      contact — is not governed by this field at all and reaches the agent under every visibility; what exposes
      an agent to them is an administrator wiring it to that surface. A refused colleague receives one short
      refusal message and no turn is started.
      A `groupId` grant is weaker here than on the assistant: this channel reads the sender's group from their
      x-bees user record, which does not always carry one. When EVERY grant on the agent is a `groupId` grant and
      the sender's group is unknown, the sender is PASSED rather than refused — refusing would lock out everyone
      whose record lacks a group, which is a large minority. Adding a `userId` or `department` grant removes that
      waiver and the agent is enforced normally, so use one of those where the restriction must hold on chat.
      (x-bees chat bots are a separate stack with their own company-level `BotAccess`; it is not this field.)

    When an agent is invoked as a background task its agent-level access is not used — invocation access is configured
    per reference on the calling agent (see AgentCallCapability.access).

items.description: A user, group or department that access is granted to.

department.description:
PBX department NAME, as carried on the colleague record (`PbxColleague.department`), not a department id.
        The x-bees directory knows a colleague's department only by name, so matching by name is what lets the check
        read a field the runtime already has instead of resolving the PBX department tree on every request.
        Two consequences: renaming a department in the PBX invalidates every grant naming it, and two departments
        with the same name in different branches of the tree are one value here.

grants.description: Users, groups and departments granted the ability to use the agent. Applies when visibility is `explicit`.

skills.description: Skills attached to this agent (progressive disclosure). A skill may carry its own tools, which join this agent's toolset while that skill is active.

id.description: Unique identifier of the tool using nanoid format

toolVersion.description: Pin a specific published tool version. When omitted, the tool's latestVersion is resolved at load, so a republished tool reaches this agent without a new agent version. Pin it when `fields` must keep aiming at an exact input schema.

description.description: Override the tool's description for this agent. When omitted, the tool's own description is used.

items.description: Per-field override applied to a shared tool's input schema for this agent.

path.description: JSON Pointer to the target property in the tool input schema.

guided.description: Keeps the field model-fillable but overrides its description in the schema shown to the model.

predefined.description: A fixed value injected at the field path and excluded from the schema shown to the model, so the model neither sees nor sets it. A JSON value, or a string with handlebars templates resolved against agent variables and session context (e.g. '{{callerName}}').

fields.description: Per-field overrides on the tool input schema: pin fixed values (hidden from the model) or refine field descriptions. Fields not listed are filled by the model per the tool schema. Paths are resolved against the input schema of the tool version in effect — pin `toolVersion` when they must not move.

startMessage.description: Message spoken when the tool call starts. Honoured on the voice channel. Spoken in every language of the call while `startMessages` is absent or empty; not consulted once `startMessages` carries any entry.

items.description:
One phrase in one language, for a capability that speaks a fixed line on the voice channel.
    Which entry is spoken is decided by the call's current language — the one the call resolved
    to at connect, or the one automatic detection switched to — matched on `language`
    CASE-INSENSITIVELY, the same rule `VoiceBotSpokenPhrase` states for the legacy stack, so a
    code written in either case reaches the same entry on either. Blank `text` means the agent
    says nothing in that language; it does NOT fall back to the language-agnostic member beside
    the list, which would speak one language's text in another language's voice.

language.description:
BCP-47 language tag, optionally with a region subtag: 'en', 'en-US', 'pt-BR'. Deliberately a
    constrained string rather than an enum: the offerable set is a property of the selected
    recogniser and changes with it, so an enumeration here would cap the set at whatever was known
    when the model was released.

startMessages.description:
Per-language start messages. When present and non-empty, the entry for the call's current
        language is spoken and `startMessage` is not consulted; a language with no entry is silent.
        When absent or empty, `startMessage` is spoken as before. On a call with no effective speech
        configuration — no configured languages, or a PBX below protocol 2 — `startMessage` is spoken
        regardless, because there is no current language to choose by.

type.description: How the model waits for a tool and whether it synthesizes a reply from the result.

instructions.description: Reply instructions for the *_GUIDED pipeline types. Use {{response}} to reference the tool result.

approval.description: Human-in-the-loop confirmation for a tool. Presence requires approval: the agent pauses before running the tool and the session user (whoever controls the session) approves or denies inline.

prompt.description: Optional message shown in the confirmation prompt. Supports handlebars against agent variables and the pending tool arguments. When omitted, a default prompt is shown.

items.description: A channel an agent can serve (see AgentChannels for enablement). Also the runtime channel recorded by the channel runtimes / wilma-traces. A background task has no delivery surface and therefore no channel.

channels.description:
Channels this capability is offered on. Absent or empty — the default — means every channel the agent serves
    that can honour it. Listing channels narrows that set and never widens it: a `transfer` listed for `chat` is
    still ignored there, because the chat channel has no call to transfer.

items.description: Configuration for annotations emitted after a tool completes.

tag.description: Tag annotation emitted after a tool completes.

value.description: Static handlebars expression resolved against agent variables and helpers.

comment.description: Comment annotation emitted after a tool completes.

value.description: Static handlebars expression resolved against agent variables and helpers.

variables.description: Variables annotation emitted after a tool completes.

result.description: Result annotation emitted after a tool completes.

connector.description:
A configured connector (wilma-tools) exposed to the model as a single meta-tool named
    after the connector. The model calls the reserved `help` action to learn the callable
    actions, then dispatches an action through the same tool. Progressive disclosure runs
    through the connector tool itself, not the skills catalogue.

id.description: Configured connector instance in wilma-tools. Its pinned definition, permission `grant` and authorization govern what the model can discover via `help` and call. There is no version pin here, unlike `AgentTool.toolVersion`: the action catalogue and its schemas are already frozen by the connector's pinned definition, while `grant` and authorization are read live so permission changes apply at once.

startMessage.description: Message spoken when a connector action call starts. Honoured on the voice channel. Mirrors `AgentTool.startMessage`. Not applied to the read-only `help` action. Not consulted once `startMessages` carries any entry.

items.description:
One phrase in one language, for a capability that speaks a fixed line on the voice channel.
    Which entry is spoken is decided by the call's current language — the one the call resolved
    to at connect, or the one automatic detection switched to — matched on `language`
    CASE-INSENSITIVELY, the same rule `VoiceBotSpokenPhrase` states for the legacy stack, so a
    code written in either case reaches the same entry on either. Blank `text` means the agent
    says nothing in that language; it does NOT fall back to the language-agnostic member beside
    the list, which would speak one language's text in another language's voice.

language.description:
BCP-47 language tag, optionally with a region subtag: 'en', 'en-US', 'pt-BR'. Deliberately a
    constrained string rather than an enum: the offerable set is a property of the selected
    recogniser and changes with it, so an enumeration here would cap the set at whatever was known
    when the model was released.

startMessages.description: Forward-compatible per-language connector start messages, mirroring `AgentTool.startMessages`. Accepted and stored so clients can configure connector and tool phrases consistently, but currently ignored at execution time because the voice runtime does not read connector start messages yet. Runtime enablement is tracked in wilma-services docs/todo.md item 8.

instructions.description: Reply instructions for the *_GUIDED pipeline types. Use {{response}} to reference the tool result.

access.description:
Who is allowed to use the agent. There is no view/edit dimension — access solely grants the ability to use the agent.

    Where it is applied, per channel:
    - `assistant` — enforced. GetAgent on wilma-assistant refuses an agent the caller is not granted.
    - `voice` — deliberately not applied. Inbound calls are routed by the PBX dialplan, and the data ACL is the
      agent-level `settings.pbxGroupId`, not per-user grants.
    - `chat` — enforced for COLLEAGUES ONLY. wilma-chat checks the sender against this block when the sender
      belongs to the agent's own company. A sender from outside it — a Kite website visitor, an SMS or WhatsApp
      contact — is not governed by this field at all and reaches the agent under every visibility; what exposes
      an agent to them is an administrator wiring it to that surface. A refused colleague receives one short
      refusal message and no turn is started.
      A `groupId` grant is weaker here than on the assistant: this channel reads the sender's group from their
      x-bees user record, which does not always carry one. When EVERY grant on the agent is a `groupId` grant and
      the sender's group is unknown, the sender is PASSED rather than refused — refusing would lock out everyone
      whose record lacks a group, which is a large minority. Adding a `userId` or `department` grant removes that
      waiver and the agent is enforced normally, so use one of those where the restriction must hold on chat.
      (x-bees chat bots are a separate stack with their own company-level `BotAccess`; it is not this field.)

    When an agent is invoked as a background task its agent-level access is not used — invocation access is configured
    per reference on the calling agent (see AgentCallCapability.access).

items.description: A user, group or department that access is granted to.

department.description:
PBX department NAME, as carried on the colleague record (`PbxColleague.department`), not a department id.
        The x-bees directory knows a colleague's department only by name, so matching by name is what lets the check
        read a field the runtime already has instead of resolving the PBX department tree on every request.
        Two consequences: renaming a department in the PBX invalidates every grant naming it, and two departments
        with the same name in different branches of the tree are one value here.

message.description: Message spoken when entering the wait state. Spoken in every language of the call while `messages` is absent or empty; not consulted once `messages` carries any entry.

items.description:
One phrase in one language, for a capability that speaks a fixed line on the voice channel.
    Which entry is spoken is decided by the call's current language — the one the call resolved
    to at connect, or the one automatic detection switched to — matched on `language`
    CASE-INSENSITIVELY, the same rule `VoiceBotSpokenPhrase` states for the legacy stack, so a
    code written in either case reaches the same entry on either. Blank `text` means the agent
    says nothing in that language; it does NOT fall back to the language-agnostic member beside
    the list, which would speak one language's text in another language's voice.

language.description:
BCP-47 language tag, optionally with a region subtag: 'en', 'en-US', 'pt-BR'. Deliberately a
    constrained string rather than an enum: the offerable set is a property of the selected
    recogniser and changes with it, so an enumeration here would cap the set at whatever was known
    when the model was released.

messages.description: Per-language wait messages. Same rule as `AgentTool.startMessages`: the entry for the call's current language is spoken, a language with no entry is silent, and with no effective speech configuration `message` is spoken.

reference.description: A resource selected as agent context, identified by its canonical URI, e.g. `wilma://insights/calls/{callId}/flows/{flowIndex}`. It is read with the permissions of the session or task it is attached to; the URI grants no access by itself.

uri.description:
Canonical URI identifying one entity on the Wilma platform, e.g. 'wilma://agents/UXDT1W9fI3sj'
    or 'wilma://skills/aB3dE5fG7hJ9'. The path names the owning service and entity kind. Opaque to
    the contracts that carry it; non-Wilma schemes (records of external systems) fit the same shape.

label.description: Display name of the mention chip. The model sees it only to name a mention that could not be read or was removed.

mentions.description: Replaces the session's mentions. Omit to keep them; pass an empty list to clear them.

items.description:
A tool the caller supplies for this session, rather than one configured on the agent. The
    routing fields (`fulfilment`, `gate`, `surface`, `stream`) are stamped onto the turn's
    InvocationStartedEvent, so clients replaying the session render the call correctly.

fulfilment.description:
Who produces an invocation's result. `server` tools execute inside the agent runtime.
    `client` tools are executed by the caller, so the turn suspends until it answers.
    `synthetic` tools never execute at all — they exist to put something on screen, and the
    runtime supplies their result itself, so the turn does not suspend.

gate.description:
Whether the turn suspends on an invocation, and for what. Orthogonal to fulfilment: a
    `server` tool may be gated on a user decision (an approval), and a `synthetic` tool may be
    ungated (render and continue) or gated (an editable draft awaiting confirmation).

surface.description: Where a client should surface an invocation. Affects placement only, never behaviour.

stream.description:
Emit InvocationDeltaEvent for calls to this tool, so the caller can render the input as the
      model writes it — useful when the input carries content rather than a lookup key. Defaults
      to false.

ack.description:
Result handed back to the model for a `synthetic` tool, typically a short instruction
      telling the model what the user can now see. Ignored for `client` tools.

items.description: Ad-hoc skill supplied by the caller for this session only.

connectors.description: Per-session connector overrides, by connector instance id. `disabled` turns connectors off for this session only; `enabled` turns back on connectors the user disabled in their settings, for this session only.

schema.description:
The editable definition of a profile: metadata plus attached features and library resources.

    A session asks a decision model at most 200 configured questions, counted across every profile
    that applies to it, a question shared by two profiles counting once: each topic category and
    topic, built-in or custom, each included signal, each intent and each evaluation. Questions copilot
    adds on its own (field guards, playbook steps, closing detection) do not count. Past the limit,
    the questions are sorted by their `<kind>.<name>` key (`evaluations.upsell`, `intents.refund`,
    `signals.escalation_requested`, `topics.billing`); those after the first 200 are not asked, and
    the session trace says which.

items.description: One audience entry: a kind, and the values of that kind the profile assists. An entry with no values does not narrow anything.

kind.description:
The kind of thing a profile is aimed at.

    Two families, and the difference decides which stages the entry can constrain.
    `user`, `group`, `department` and `agent` name **who is assisted** - a person for the first
    three, a Wilma AI agent for the last - and in the `before` stage the assisted party is
    whoever opened copilot, so they constrain every stage. `queue`, `service` and `trunk`
    describe a **live conversation**, which does not exist in `before` - so an entry of those
    kinds says nothing there.

    Values are the tenant's own routing objects: user emails for `user`, Wilma agent ids for
    `agent`, PBX group and department ids, queue and trunk names as `wda-stream` reports them,
    and x-bees service uris for `service`.

audience.description:
Who this profile assists - queues, groups, departments, users, AI agents, chat services
        and trunks. Empty or absent means everyone in the company. This is the profile's primary
        scope: an administrator reaches for "my refunds team", not for a conversation medium,
        and a queue already carries the medium, the skill and the line of business.

stages.description: Stages of a conversation this profile applies in. Empty or absent means every stage.

items.description:

channels.description:

sentiment.description: Configuration for the built-in sentiment feature.

talkRatio.description: Configuration for the built-in talk ratio feature.

topics.description:
Configuration for the built-in topics feature.

    Topics are classified, not summarised: a decision model answers, for each category and topic,
    whether the conversation covers it, and `topics` holds the names of the categories and topics it
    does - values a condition can compare. A category is asked on every full-transcript pass until it
    is detected; its topics are asked once it is. A category's name is in `topics` when the category
    itself is detected, not when one of its topics is.

    `custom` adds the company's own: new categories with their topics, and topics added to a
    built-in category, such as `mastercard` in `payment`. Each category and topic, built-in or
    custom, counts towards the session's question limit.

    in one. The catalog lives with the service, which rejects a name it does not know, so new groups
    and labels need no SDK release. A company's own topic categories and topics use the same form.

custom.description:

signals.description:

    catalog has three groups:

    - `moments`: moments that need someone now, such as an escalation request, a legal threat or a
      repeat contact. Asked when a customer turn ends.

items.description:
One phrase in one language, for a capability that speaks a fixed line on the voice channel.
    Which entry is spoken is decided by the call's current language — the one the call resolved
    to at connect, or the one automatic detection switched to — matched on `language`
    CASE-INSENSITIVELY, the same rule `VoiceBotSpokenPhrase` states for the legacy stack, so a
    code written in either case reaches the same entry on either. Blank `text` means the agent
    says nothing in that language; it does NOT fall back to the language-agnostic member beside
    the list, which would speak one language's text in another language's voice.

language.description:
BCP-47 language tag, optionally with a region subtag: 'en', 'en-US', 'pt-BR'. Deliberately a
    constrained string rather than an enum: the offerable set is a property of the selected
    recogniser and changes with it, so an enumeration here would cap the set at whatever was known
    when the model was released.

startMessages.description:

        language is spoken and `startMessage` is not consulted; a language with no entry is silent.
        When absent or empty, `startMessage` is spoken as before. On a call with no effective speech
        configuration — no configured languages, or a PBX below protocol 2 — `startMessage` is spoken
        regardless, because there is no current language to choose by.

    and reference it at the same path.

handler.description: Handler of the tool. connector.description:
Handler for a connector-backed Tool created through `CreateTool`. Carries two
configuration layers: `configuration` (from the mixin) holds definition-level values for
the connector as a whole (validated against the definition `configuration.schema`), while
`toolConfiguration` holds values specific to this created Tool (validated against the
pinned connector tool's `configuration.schema`).

`Tool.input` follows copy-at-create semantics: when `input` is omitted on create, the
service snapshots the pinned connector tool's input schema into the Tool; callers may
instead provide — and later edit — a custom schema. The Tool owns its copy; definition
changes never propagate to existing tools. Reshaping the input of a tool whose handler
does not consume input through configuration templates fails at execution, not at write.

items.description:
Reference to one wilma-tools-backed agent capability to describe: either a standalone
Tool or a configured Connector.

The two members are deliberately asymmetric. A Tool is a model-facing contract — its input
schema is what the model fills, and agents pin JSON Pointers into it — so it is versioned and
referenced by `ToolRef`. A Connector exposes no schema at reference time: the model discovers
actions at runtime through the reserved `help` action, and every action, schema and document it
can reach is already frozen by the connector's pinned `ConnectorDefinitionRef`. A configured
connector therefore needs no version history of its own and is referenced by id.

is typically an object with exactly one connector tool id key and argument object.

`help` is a reserved action returning guidance in `result.output`; nothing external is
dispatched, and a definition must not declare a tool with id `help`:
  - `{"help": {}}` — index: the connector's `instructions`, the enabled actions grouped
    by `category` (id, name, one-line description, access), and the list of reference
    documents (name + summary).
  - `{"help": {"action": "<toolId>"}}` — detail for one action: full input schema,
    `examples`, and `docs`.
  - `{"help": {"reference": "<name>"}}` — the full body of one reference document.
  - `{"help": {"category": "<name>"}}` — details for every action in a category.

schema.description:
Trace filters, one per entry; a trace matches when every entry holds.

        - `key=value`: the Trace.attributes value equals `value`, e.g. `filter=channel%3Dvoice`.
        - `key=*`: the attribute is present with a non-empty value, e.g. `filter=call.transferTo%3D*`.
        - `metric>=N` / `metric<=N`: an inclusive bound on a Trace.metrics value, e.g.
          `filter=durationMs%3E%3D60000`; both bounds on one metric give a window. A trace that
          carries no value for the metric matches no bound, so `usage.interruptions<=0` does not
          find a trace that never recorded it. `durationMs` is the trace's own wall-clock length:
          every ended trace has it, a pending one never does.

        `*` always means presence, so a literal `*` value cannot be matched; `key=` matches an
        empty value; when one key is given twice, the last entry wins. `N` is a plain decimal
        (`-12`, `0.5`) within ±9007199254740991 (2^53−1).

        Any other entry is a 400 ValidationException that names it: an empty entry, one with no
        `=`, one with nothing before `=` (`=x`), a reversed bound (`durationMs=>N`), strict `>` or
        `<`, a bound on a name that is not a trace metric, `key=value` on a metric name (bound it
        with `>=`/`<=` instead), and an `N` that is not a plain decimal
        (`0x10`, `1e3`) or lies outside that range.

get.description:
Tails a live call's events as Server-Sent Events (`text/event-stream`): the caller's recognised speech, the agent's spoken sentences, playback, interruptions, language switches and the session lifecycle. Live only — nothing before the subscription is replayed, and the stream is not a record of the call (the session trace is). Ends after an `ended` event whose reason is not `transfer`; after a transfer it stays open briefly for the next session of the same call. What the stream carries is decided HERE, by who is asking, and is not a request parameter: a caller signed in to the system receives everything, including the agent's own commands (`reply`, `say`, `playback`, `interruption`) and its tool calls, and chooses for itself what to show; a guest receives the transcript alone (`started`, `transcription`, `agentTranscription`, `language`, `ended`).

post.description:
Synthesizes one phrase and returns MP3.

    NOT NAMED FOR THE PREVIEW IT SERVES. Auditioning an unsaved voice in the console is the first
    caller, but nothing about the operation is preview-specific — it is the platform's
    text-to-speech, reachable by anything holding the scope, and a name naming one caller's screen
    would have to be worked around by the second one.

    EVERYTHING TRAVELS IN THE REQUEST and the operation reads no stored record — not the agent, and
    no dictionary behind it. The settings being auditioned are unsaved form state, and the rules
    that apply are the ones on `pronunciations`, so what is heard here is what the call would say.

### Allowed Auth Scopes

- wilma-voice:TextToSpeech

voice.description: Voice to speak with, as the URI a call would use — provider, voice id, synthesis parameters and, for a company's own account, `apiKey=secrets:{secretId}`. Passing the call's own value is what keeps an audition from diverging from the call it is auditioning.

language.description: Language the phrase is in. Reaches the provider as the synthesis language, and is the language `pronunciations` was written for.

text.description: Text to speak, BEFORE pronunciation rules are applied.

items.description:
A pronunciation rule for one phrase. Belongs to a LANGUAGE, not to the agent: 'Wildix' is
    respelled differently for an Italian and a German voice, so one list shared ACROSS languages
    would fight itself. That is why the rules hang off the language and nowhere else — there is no
    company-wide dictionary above them to inherit from, or to disagree with.

phrase.description: The phrase as it appears in the text, e.g. 'Wildix'. Bounded because every rule is compiled into ONE regular expression — see the list below.

encoding.description: How the `as` member of a pronunciation rule is written.

pronunciations.description: Rules to apply to `text`, applied SERVER-SIDE by the same helper the call path uses — never pre-applied by the caller, or the form reimplements a rule the server owns and can silently diverge from the call. Pass the language's own list to hear exactly what a call would say.

A reference to the company's own provider credential, so the picker lists that account's
      voices including cloned ones. Absent means the platform key.

      `secrets:{secretId}` ONLY, resolved under the CALLER's company — an id that does not resolve
      there is rejected. There is no form of this member that carries a key, which is what keeps a
      provider credential out of a URL on this stack: every one of them lives in `wilma-secrets`,
      and a reference in a query string is not a secret.

      A stored voice URI says the same thing the same way: its `apiKey` parameter is a reference,
      and `validateSpeech` refuses a literal key in one.
